chapter: Bill Robinson and Chuck and Chuckles
title: The Pretty Foot and 24-bar choruses
summary: Green explains Robinson's moving toe step, the Pretty Foot, and that Depression-era choruses were 24 bars with a two-bar intro.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Super. Super. Well, Chuck, one would think that actually was Bill Bojangles, because it's so perfect. Your footwork is so perfect. I've seen him many times, fortunately, on the movies, and I mean your feet are exactly like his.

Yes. Well, he would only allow the best you could do. If he taught you any tap step. And he never would teach you an entire tap dance routine. He would teach you how to begin to tap dancing, see? And you would have to either buy a ticket or wait till he'd bring some tickets around the Tree of Hope, or you could go into the lobby of the theater or wherever he was playing in New York City at that time, and see him tap dance. And try to learn yourself some of the tap steps.
He must be very pleased with you. The step that you do where you draw your toes back and you draw it back and hit the toe --
Yeah. He called that a lower. That was getting the straw first for the hula. Haloha.

Yes, that is. And he did it circularly. That's why you hear the moving. It's supposed to be -- convey the sound of like the propellors going off or the ship putting on brakes, you see. You hear the turbulence.
I know you're very fond of that step and you carry it with you wherever you go.
Because we see you use it -- you still use that up to today, here and there.
Well, what does that step do for you as a performer? Like how do you feel when you're doing it? Why do you add it in at certain moments?

Well, because the most important sound in tap dancing is the moving. If you're tap dancing and you begin to moving as you're tap dancing, that's considered travelling. And as I was saying, that's one of his first routines. See, he numbered each one of his tap dances, like one, two, three, four, up to 26. Because musically, in those times, those days, the tap dancer was allowed two bars of music introduction. And then a 24 bar chorus of music was considered one chorus, instead of 32 bars. Because, as I said before, they were working on the Depression, see, so they tried to do the best -- most of the best right away, abruptly, see, that's to keep the
nation, the people, from getting into a lull again, or starting to getting disastrous thoughts about their life.
And of course, tap dancing being the music of the feet, a step like that, the one where you make that sound where you draw your foot back and hit your toe, this is just another musical tone or sound.
That adds to all the pretty sounds that we do make with the feet.
